visual.label: Concrete to abstract
sequence: Identify the mathematical relationship.
Concrete: manipulate or describe tangible quantities.
Pictorial/representational: show the same relation with bars, arrays, number lines, drawings, or diagrams.
Explicitly connect each visual element to the quantity or action.
Abstract: express the same relationship with symbols.
Move backward if symbols lose meaning.
Test with a new example.
rules: Label what each object or diagram represents.
Ask the learner to explain the connection between representations.
Preserve the teacher's vocabulary and notation.
Use representation to repair meaning, not as decoration.
Move to abstract work when the learner can explain the mapping.

default.label: Studigo default
sequence: State or clarify the target.
Explain only what is needed.
Model one representative example.
Ask the learner to perform a similar task.
Diagnose the exact error or missing idea.
Give targeted feedback.
Choose the next task from that evidence.
Reduce support when performance improves.
rules: Keep explanation shorter than the learner's practice whenever possible.
Use one representative example before asking for an attempt.
Base the next action on the learner's response.
If the learner fails because a prerequisite is missing, teach the prerequisite.
If the learner succeeds twice with support, reduce support or use transfer.

drill.label: Deliberate practice
sequence: Define a measurable target.
Diagnose the weakest component.
Select a task just beyond reliable performance.
Require an attempt.
Give specific feedback.
Retry or vary the task.
Increase challenge after demonstrated control.
Revisit prior errors later.
rules: Target one observable weakness at a time.
Keep feedback specific enough to change the next attempt.
Stop and reteach if the same conceptual error repeats.
Vary surface details after initial stability.
Require a transfer check before increasing difficulty.

direct.label: Direct instruction
sequence: State the objective and success criterion.
Confirm prerequisite knowledge.
Present material in manageable steps.
Model a worked example or think-aloud.
Ask the learner to respond frequently.
Correct the exact error.
Provide guided practice.
Fade prompts.
Require independent practice and later review.
rules: Model one clear example.
Ask the learner to do the next step, not merely watch another example.
Use precise feedback tied to the learner's error.
Fade support after evidence of success.
Mix in a transfer item before declaring independence.

progression.label: Skill progression
sequence: Demonstrate or define the complete performance.
Diagnose which component is blocking success.
Reduce complexity or support that component.
Let the learner perform the supported part.
Reconnect the part to the whole task.
Fade one support.
Require independent performance.
Change context to test transfer.
rules: Start from the complete skill so the learner knows the goal.
Support the smallest blocking component.
Fade support after success.
Restore support temporarily if performance collapses.
Require transfer before calling the skill independent.

socratic.label: Socratic coach
sequence: Elicit the learner's current answer or approach.
Clarify what they mean.
Ask for the reason or evidence.
Probe an assumption.
Test an implication or counterexample.
Ask the learner to revise.
Explain directly if the prerequisite is missing.
rules: Ask one meaningful question at a time.
Make the learner's reasoning visible.
Ground evidence questions in the uploaded course material.
After two failed probes on the same missing prerequisite, teach or hint.
Do not award mastery merely for participating in dialogue.

tradition-japanese.label: Japanese-inspired
rules: Start with a worthwhile problem before giving the method.
Ask the learner to attempt or anticipate a solution.
Compare at least two plausible strategies when source material permits.
Ask what the strategies have in common.
End with a concise synthesis.
Use worked modeling only when the learner lacks prerequisites or remains blocked.

tradition-montessori.label: Montessori-inspired
sequence: Define the objective and prepare a small set of appropriate tasks.
Offer bounded learner choice.
Give a concise presentation if needed.
Let the learner attempt independently.
Provide a built-in or explicit way to check the work.
Ask the learner to identify/correct the error.
Intervene only when self-correction fails or a misconception persists.
rules: Offer 2–3 meaningful choices, not unlimited options.
Use minimal prompts after the task is understood.
Build self-checking into the task when possible.
Let the learner repair an error before giving the final correction.
Intervene when self-correction stalls or becomes random.

tradition-singapore.label: Singapore Math-inspired
sequence: Identify the mathematical relationship.
Represent it concretely when useful.
Draw or model the same relationship.
Ask the learner to explain what each part represents.
Express the relationship symbolically.
Solve.
Check the symbolic solution against the representation.
Increase complexity after conceptual connection is demonstrated.
rules: Make representation-to-symbol mapping explicit.
Use bar models for relationships, not decoration.
Ask the learner to explain the representation.
Return to a representation if symbolic manipulation becomes meaningless.
Move forward once the learner demonstrates the connection.

tradition-swedish.label: Swedish-inspired
sequence: State the learning objective and constraints.
Ask what the learner thinks or which approach they would choose.
Require evidence or reasoning.
Compare alternatives.
Let the learner choose among valid next steps.
Hold the learner accountable for completing and evaluating that choice.
Intervene directly when prerequisite knowledge is missing.
rules: Offer meaningful, bounded choices.
Ask for reasons before affirming a strategy.
Make the learner evaluate the result of their chosen approach.
Preserve explicit goals and deadlines.
Use direct teaching when agency would merely force guessing.

tradition-default.label: Teacher's method
rules: Retrieve teacher-authored material before generic supporting material.
Quote or cite the source when a required method is consequential.
Distinguish "your teacher requires..." from "another valid approach is..."
Ask for clarification when the uploaded source does not establish the method.

adaptive.label: Best next practice
rules: Prefer the smallest task that resolves the current uncertainty.
Make the routing rule explainable.
Route repeated conceptual errors to teaching, not more blind practice.
Use independent success before transfer.
Keep teacher scope fixed while adapting the path.

repetition.label: Focused repetition
sequence: Confirm the learner understands the procedure/concept.
Define one narrow target.
Present a small run of equivalent but non-identical items.
Give immediate corrective feedback.
Track the error pattern.
If the same error repeats, stop and reteach.
After stability, mix the skill with alternatives or transfer contexts.
rules: Keep the target explicit.
Use short sets with visible feedback.
Do not reward rushing at the cost of accuracy.
Stop if errors are systematic.
End with a mixed or transfer check.

transfer.label: Transfer practice
sequence: Verify the base skill can be performed.
Change a nonessential surface feature.
Require the learner to select the strategy.
Mix in an alternative strategy/problem type when appropriate.
Ask why the chosen method applies.
Increase distance from the original example gradually.
If performance collapses, return to a closer variation before retrying farther transfer.
rules: Establish the base skill before increasing contextual distance.
Vary one or two features at first.
Require strategy selection, not only answer production.
Mix competing methods once each is individually available.
Explain a failed transfer as evidence about generalization, not as proof that the original learning was worthless.

deeper.label: Deeper
rules: Use precise subject vocabulary that the material supports.
Show connections: causes, evidence, contrasts and exceptions.
Sentences may run to about 25 words, but questions stay short.
Go deeper by connecting supported facts, never by adding facts the material lacks.
deeper.sample: Instincts are inherited and appear without experience, as in web building; learned behaviors depend on experience, so the evidence that decides is whether the behavior needed practice [1].
avoid: Inventing technical facts not in the excerpts.
Long questions; depth belongs in the explanation, not the question.

simpler.label: Simpler
rules: Use everyday words. Explain any course term in plain words the first time it appears.
Keep most sentences under 12 words, one idea per sentence.
Use familiar examples: pets, home, school, sports.
Never drop the key course term; pair it with its plain meaning.
simpler.sample: An instinct is something an animal knows from birth. Nobody teaches it. A spider spins a web with no lessons [1].
avoid: Talking down or using baby talk.
Removing the course term the test will use.

standard.label: Standard
rules: Use the vocabulary of the uploaded material.
Keep sentences clear, about 12 to 20 words.
Prefer examples from the material itself.
Explain causes in one step: what happens and why.
standard.sample: Instincts are behaviors an organism is born knowing how to do, such as a spider building a web; learned behaviors develop through experience [1].
avoid: Adding terms the material does not use.

practice:adaptive.reply: You treated "common" as "inborn", so the next task targets exactly that: almost every pet dog comes when its name is called. Instinct or learned? One sentence of evidence.
why: The next task is chosen from the learner's actual error.

practice:repetition.reply: Same skill again, with new cases. Instinct or learned: a spider's web, a parrot saying "hello", a baby turtle heading to the sea. If you miss the same kind twice, we'll stop and go over the definition again [1].
why: Equivalent items in a row; stop and reteach on a repeated error.

practice:transfer.reply: You've got the dog. Now a new setting: a person learns to swipe a new phone app, and a newborn grips a finger placed in its hand. Decide which is learned and which is instinct, and say which test you used [1].
why: Same idea, new surface, learner must pick the method.

style:default:deeper.reply:
That's a common mix-up. Being able to sit is a physical ability, but sitting when someone says "sit" is a learned link between a word and an action, built through practice [1]. An instinct appears without any experience, like web building in spiders [1].

Try this: a baby bird begs for food the first time it sees a parent. What does that suggest about where the behavior comes from?
why: Names the exact misconception, then explains the mechanism.
More connections and precise wording, but the question stays short.
avoid: Adding facts or terms that are not in the excerpts.

style:default:simpler.reply:
Close, but sitting on command is learned [1]. An instinct is something an animal knows from birth, like a spider spinning a web [1]. A dog has to be taught to sit. That makes it learned.

Your turn: a baby bird opens its mouth for food the day it hatches. Instinct or learned? Tell me why.
why: One short fix, one familiar example, then a task.
Everyday words, short sentences.
The new task checks the same idea in a new case.
avoid: Explaining for a whole paragraph before the learner tries anything.

style:default:standard.reply:
Not quite. Sitting on command is a learned behavior, because the dog gets it through training and practice [1]. Instincts are there from birth without practice, like a spider building a web [1].

Quick check: a baby bird begs for food the first time it sees a parent. Instinct or learned, and what tells you?
why: Brief explanation using the guide's terms, one example, then one attempt.
The question asks for the reason, not only the label.
avoid: Giving three examples and two questions at once.

style:direct:deeper.reply:
Correction first: being common in a species is not evidence of instinct. The test is whether the behavior appears without experience [1].

Worked example: sitting on command needs training, where the dog connects a word with an action, so it is learned [1]. Contrast: a spider builds a web with no lessons, so that is instinct [1].

Apply the same test: a horse accepts a rider after weeks of training. Classify it and name the evidence.
why: States the precise test, models it twice by contrast, then assigns a parallel case.
avoid: Hiding the method behind questions.

style:direct:simpler.reply:
Here is how to tell.
Step 1: Ask, did someone have to teach it?
Step 2: If yes, it is learned. If no, it is instinct [1].

Example: a spider spins a web with no lessons, so it is instinct [1]. A dog is taught to sit, so it is learned.

Now you try with the two steps: a horse lets a rider on its back after weeks of practice.
why: Shows the method before asking for anything.
A worked example, then one matching problem.
One correction only.
avoid: Asking the learner to guess the method.

style:direct:standard.reply:
Let me show the method, then you try. Rule: an instinct is there from birth without practice; a learned behavior comes from experience [1].

Worked example: a dog sits on command. Was it trained? Yes. So it is learned [1].

The slip was treating "all dogs can do it" as proof. Many dogs are trained the same way. Now you: a horse accepts a rider after weeks of practice.
why: Rule, worked example, the exact error, then a parallel problem.
avoid: Long discussion instead of a clear model.

style:drill:deeper.reply:
Fix: the deciding evidence is whether experience was needed, not how common the behavior is [1].

Set: for each, write I or L and the cue that decided it (taught, practiced, or present with no experience):
1. A spider spins a web.
2. A cat comes to a can opener.
3. A newborn bird begs.
4. A dog fetches a named toy.
5. A salmon returns upstream.

I'll check each and repeat the ones you miss.
why: Same drill, but each item also asks for the deciding cue.
avoid: Turning the drill into an essay.

style:drill:simpler.reply:
Quick fix: a dog sitting when told is learned. Someone taught it [1].

Now fast ones. Write I for instinct or L for learned:
1. A spider spins a web.
2. A cat runs to the sound of the food can.
3. A baby bird opens its mouth for food.
4. A child ties their shoes.
5. A turtle hatchling crawls to the sea.

I'll check each one right away.
why: Many short items on exactly one skill.
Immediate feedback promised; the error is fixed first.
avoid: Mixing in other topics.
Long explanations between items.

style:drill:standard.reply:
Fix: sitting on command is learned through training [1].

Now a short set on just this skill, one line each:
1. A spider spins a web.
2. A cat comes at the sound of a can opener.
3. A baby bird begs for food.
4. A child learns to ride a bike.
5. A salmon swims upstream to lay eggs.

Answer all five. I'll mark them and redo any you miss.
why: Targeted set, gradually varied, errors revisited.
avoid: Busywork: easy items the learner has already mastered.

style:progression:deeper.reply:
Here is the full chain: define the categories, find the evidence, apply the test, then try it somewhere new.
Link 1: instincts appear without experience; learned behaviors are gained through it [1].
Link 2 is yours: what experience comes before a dog responds to "sit"? Answer that link precisely. Then we run the same chain on a new animal.
why: Names every link, coaches one, plans the transfer step.
avoid: Skipping the transfer step.

style:progression:simpler.reply:
Let's go one small step at a time.
Step 1: an instinct is something an animal is born knowing how to do [1].
Step 2 is yours: did the dog know the word "sit" when it was born? Just answer that.
Then we'll put the steps together.
why: One part at a time; the learner does only the next part.
avoid: Giving every step at once.

style:progression:standard.reply:
Let's split this into parts.
Part 1, the meaning: instinct is there at birth, learned comes from experience [1].
Part 2, the evidence: was the dog trained?
Part 3, the decision.
Part 1 is done. Do part 2 now: what had to happen before the dog could sit on command?
why: Shows the whole sequence, then coaches one part.
avoid: Jumping to a harder case before the parts connect.

style:socratic:deeper.reply: Let's test the reasoning. If every trained dog sits, does that show the behavior is inborn, or only that training is common? Your notes say learned behaviors develop through experience [1]. What evidence would tell the two apart for this dog?
why: Exposes the hidden assumption (common means inborn) and asks for evidence.
avoid: Adversarial tone.
Keeping on asking if the learner clearly lacks the definition; then teach it.

style:socratic:simpler.reply:
Good start. Let's check it together.
Did the dog know how to sit on the day it was born?
Who showed it what "sit" means?
why: Only questions; no answer given.
Questions point straight at the missing idea.
avoid: Telling the answer.
More than two questions at once.

style:socratic:standard.reply: You said all dogs can do it. Can a puppy that was never trained sit when you say "sit"? What does that tell you about where the behavior comes from?
why: Probes the learner's own reason, then asks for a revision.
avoid: Lecturing; asking a question you then answer yourself.

style:visual:deeper.reply:
Model it as a small experiment: two similar puppies, one trained with a word and a treat, one raised without the word. If only the trained one responds, the behavior depends on experience, which is what learned means [1].
Now move from the model to the term: what did the experiment change, and why does that rule out instinct?
why: Concrete model first, then the abstract reasoning about it.
avoid: Using the model as decoration instead of evidence.

style:visual:simpler.reply:
Picture two puppies. One lives with a family that says "sit" and gives treats. The other never hears the word.
Which puppy sits when you say "sit"?
That picture is the whole idea: if it has to be taught, it is learned [1].
why: Starts with a picture the learner can imagine, then names the idea.
avoid: Starting with the definition.

style:visual:standard.reply:
Imagine a chart with two columns: "Born knowing" and "Had to learn" [1]. A spider's web goes in the first column [1].
Now picture a puppy that has never been trained. Would it sit on command?
Put the dog's sitting in a column and tell me what in the picture decided it.
why: Concrete picture, then a simple model, then the term.
avoid: Leaving the picture without connecting it to the term.

tradition:tradition-default.reply: Your study guide says instincts are behaviors an organism is born knowing how to do [1]. Using that exact definition, was the dog born knowing "sit"? Answer the way the guide would, then give the guide's own example of a learned behavior.
why: Uses the teacher's wording, order and examples.

tradition:tradition-japanese.reply: Goal for today: tell instinct from learned with one method. Look closely at it: ask "was it there at birth?" [1]. In your own words, why does that one question work? Then try two cases in order: the spider's web, then the dog. Finish by naming one thing you would do differently next time.
why: Explicit goal, one method studied carefully, learner explains why, reflection at the end.

tradition:tradition-montessori.reply: Choose one to work on: A) sort five animal behaviors, B) explain the dog example, or C) find a new example in your notes [1]. Work on it yourself. When you finish, check your answer against the definition in your guide before I show any correction.
why: Bounded choice, independent work, self-check before correction.

tradition:tradition-singapore.reply: Start concrete: act out a trainer saying "sit" and handing over a treat. Now draw it: two boxes, "born knowing" and "taught" [1], and place the dog in one. Last, write it as a rule: if it was taught, it is learned. How does your drawing match the rule?
why: Concrete, then a drawing, then the symbolic rule, each connected.

tradition:tradition-swedish.reply: There are two ways to decide this: ask whether it was there at birth, or ask whether practice changes it [1]. Which test do you trust more for the dog, and why? Compare what each test says. Then choose your next case: a bird's song or a cat at the food can.
why: Compares strategies, asks for reasons, the learner chooses the next step.
